echoes.note: Jesus 'went up onto the mountain' to teach Torah, evoking Moses ascending Sinai to receive the law; Matthew presents a new-Moses giving authoritative instruction from a mountain.
Moses summoned up the mountain to receive the tablets of law and commandment; the Sermon's mountain setting figurally recasts the giving of Torah.
Moses assembles and teaches Israel the statutes; the seated Teacher addressing disciples mirrors the Mosaic instruction frame.
'The gentle/meek shall inherit the earth/land' is a near-verbatim echo of LXX Ps 36:11 (Ps 37:11), the clearest single source behind the third beatitude.

Isaiah's anointed proclaims good news to the poor and comfort to all who mourn; multiple beatitudes (poor, mourning-comforted, righteousness) cluster on this Servant text, which Jesus elsewhere claims.
God dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit; 'poor in spirit' draws on this prophetic ideal of humble dependence on God.
God regards the poor, contrite in spirit, who tremble at his word — background for 'blessed are the poor in spirit.'
The LORD is near the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit; coheres with poor-in-spirit and those who mourn.
The mourners shall possess a double portion and everlasting joy; reinforces the inheritance/reward logic of the beatitudes.
'Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? ... He who has clean hands and a pure heart' — direct source for 'blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.'
'God is good to the pure in heart' — recurrent Psalter theme behind the sixth beatitude.
'Blessed is the man...' — the makarism/beatitude form itself is rooted in the Psalter's wisdom blessing formula.
Beatitude-form blessing ('Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven'); shapes the genre of Jesus' blessings.
The redeemed 'shall not hunger nor thirst'; background for 'hunger and thirst after righteousness ... shall be filled.'
God satisfies the hungry and thirsty soul; coheres with the fourth beatitude's promise of being filled.
'Blessed is he who is generous/merciful to the poor'; wisdom background for 'blessed are the merciful.'
'I desire mercy'; the mercy-receives-mercy logic of the fifth beatitude resonates with Hosea, a text Matthew cites twice elsewhere.
To do justice, love mercy (hesed), walk humbly — clusters mercy, righteousness, and humility that pervade the beatitudes.
'I shall behold your face in righteousness' — beatific seeing of God promised to the pure in heart.
Jacob saw God face to face and lived; background to the extraordinary promise 'they shall see God.'
The saints of the Most High receive and possess the kingdom; underwrites 'theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven' (bracketing beatitudes 1 and 8).
Kingdom and dominion given to the people of the holy ones; reinforces the kingdom-inheritance frame.
Israel as God's 'children'/friends; background for peacemakers 'called children of God.'
'You are children of the living God' — divine-sonship language behind 'they shall be called children of God.'
'Seek peace and pursue it'; the active peacemaking blessed in the seventh beatitude.
Israel mocked and persecuted the prophets; basis for 'so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.'
Elijah laments the slaying of the prophets; the persecuted-prophets motif of v.12.
The prophet Uriah killed for prophesying; concrete instance of persecuted prophets behind v.12.
'Fear not the reproach of men' addressed to those with God's law in their heart — close parallel to being reproached/reviled for righteousness' sake.
The wicked plot against the righteous one, reproaching and persecuting him to test his patience; Second Temple background for the persecuted-righteous beatitudes.
Elijah among the persecuted prophets; deuterocanonical recollection of the prophets' suffering invoked in v.12.
Those who sow in tears reap with joy; coheres with mourners being comforted and rejoicing.
Deuterocanonical exhortation to mercy/almsgiving that obtains divine favor; background to 'blessed are the merciful.'
The 'salt of the covenant' required with every grain offering; salt as covenant-fidelity image behind 'you are the salt of the earth.'
'A covenant of salt forever' — salt symbolizing enduring covenant loyalty, the failure of which (losing savor) is the warning.
Davidic kingship given by a 'covenant of salt'; reinforces salt's covenantal connotation.
The Servant made 'a light to the nations/world' — direct background for 'you are the light of the world,' extending Israel's vocation to the disciples.
The Servant given 'as a light to the nations'; reinforces the light-to-the-world commission.
Zion's light arises and nations come to its brightness; a city/light that cannot be hidden draws on this eschatological imagery.
The mountain of the LORD's house lifted up, with nations streaming to it; 'a city set on a hill cannot be hidden' evokes the eschatological Zion.
The wise 'shall shine like the brightness of the firmament'; the radiance of the righteous behind 'let your light shine.'
The path of the righteous is like the dawning light that grows brighter; wisdom image of righteous luminance.
When justice is done, 'your light shall break forth like the dawn'; light as visible righteous deeds (cf. 'see your good works').
Doing good to the afflicted causes one's light to rise in darkness — coheres with light shining through good works.
Do not add to or take from the commandment; 'not one jot or tittle shall pass' affirms the law's inviolability in the same spirit.
Warning against adding to or diminishing God's commands; background to the permanence of every least commandment.
'The grass withers... but the word of our God stands forever'; heaven-and-earth-may-pass-but-the-law-endures echoes the abiding word.
'The heavens shall vanish... but my salvation shall be forever' — direct background for 'until heaven and earth pass away, not one letter shall pass from the law.'
'Forever, O LORD, your word is settled in the heavens'; the eternal stability of Torah affirmed in v.18.
'Every one of your righteous ordinances endures forever'; coheres with the permanence of the least commandments.
'The law... endures forever' — Second Temple affirmation of Torah's eternity behind v.18.
Call to keep and not depart from God's statutes; resonates with not breaking the least commandments.
'You shall not murder' — verbatim citation of the sixth commandment (Decalogue) introduced by the antithesis formula.
Parallel Decalogue form of 'You shall not murder'; the cited commandment stands in both Exodus and Deuteronomy.
Bloodshed brings judgment ('whoever sheds man's blood...'); background for 'whoever murders shall be liable to judgment.'
Mosaic law on the murderer being put to death by the court; 'liable to the judgment/council' draws on this judicial framework.
Hard cases of bloodshed brought before judges/priests; the escalating tribunal (judgment, council) reflects Israel's courts.
'You shall not hate your brother in your heart' — the interiorizing of murder into anger toward 'your brother' draws on the Holiness Code.
Prohibition of grudge-bearing against one's kin; coheres with reconciling before offering one's gift.
Cain's anger toward his brother culminating in murder is the archetype of the anger-to-murder continuum Jesus expounds.
Wisdom on settling with one's adversary before wrath/ruin; background for 'agree with your adversary quickly... lest he hand you to the judge.'
'Do not hastily bring to court... settle your case with your neighbor'; coheres with vv.25-26's counsel to reconcile en route.
God rejects sacrifice from those whose hands are unjust until they do right; prophetic priority of reconciliation over cultic gift (vv.23-24).
God despises offerings divorced from justice; background to leaving one's gift to be reconciled first.
'You shall not commit adultery' — verbatim citation of the seventh commandment.
Parallel Decalogue form of the adultery prohibition.
'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife' — the interiorizing of adultery into lustful looking draws directly on the coveting commandment.
'I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?' — the closest parallel to lustful looking already being sin.
If my heart followed my eyes — the eye-heart link Jesus develops ('looks with lust... in his heart').
'Do not desire her beauty in your heart, nor let her capture you with her eyelashes' — wisdom on lust of the eyes/heart.
Potiphar's wife 'cast her eyes' on Joseph; the gaze-leading-to-adultery motif.
'Turn away your eyes from a shapely woman... many have been led astray by a woman's beauty' — Second Temple wisdom on the lustful gaze.
Prayer against the lust of the eyes and sinful desire; coheres with guarding the eye against lust.
Even a beloved relation must be cut off if leading to sin; background to the radical 'pluck out the eye, cut off the hand.'
'Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce' — direct citation of the Mosaic divorce provision Jesus qualifies.
The fuller divorce-and-remarriage statute; Jesus reframes its concession around the cause of immorality.
'The two become one flesh' — the creation order of marriage underlies Jesus' restriction of divorce (made explicit in Mt 19).
God hates divorce / the treacherous putting-away of a wife; prophetic background to Jesus' tightening of the divorce concession.
'You shall not swear by my name falsely' — direct source for 'you shall not swear falsely.'
'When a man vows a vow to the LORD... he shall do all that proceeds from his mouth' — basis for 'but shall perform to the Lord your vows.'
Vows to the LORD must be paid and not delayed; reinforces the obligation-to-perform clause Jesus cites.
'You shall not take the name of the LORD in vain' — the Decalogue prohibition behind false/empty swearing.
Who has not 'sworn deceitfully' — the false-oath concern of the oath antithesis (and ties to the pure in heart of v.8).
'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool' — direct source for swearing 'neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; nor by the earth, his footstool.'
Zion 'the city of the great King' — direct source for 'nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.'
'The LORD's throne is in heaven'; coheres with heaven as God's throne, making oaths by it oaths by God.
Better not to vow than to vow and not pay; wisdom critique of rash vows behind 'swear not at all.'
'Do not accustom your mouth to oaths' — Second Temple wisdom counseling against habitual swearing, closely parallel to v.34.
Human powerlessness to effect things by one's word; coheres with 'you cannot make one hair white or black' (v.36).
'Eye for eye, tooth for tooth' — verbatim citation of the lex talionis Jesus sets in antithesis.
'Fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth' — parallel talion formula behind the citation.
'Eye for eye, tooth for tooth' — third Pentateuchal statement of the talion principle.
'Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him' — close parallel to 'turn the other cheek.'
The Servant 'gave my back to those who strike, my cheeks to those who pull the beard' — nonretaliatory suffering behind turning the cheek.
'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD' — wisdom renunciation of retaliation behind 'do not resist the evildoer.'
'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me' — direct rejection of tit-for-tat, paralleling the non-resistance teaching.
Feed your enemy, give him drink; the generous-to-the-aggressor ethic extending into giving coat and cloak.
The cloak taken in pledge must be returned; legal background sharpening 'let him have your cloak also.'
Do not harden your heart but open your hand to the poor and lend freely; direct background to 'give to him who asks, do not refuse the borrower.'
Give freely and open your hand to the needy; reinforces v.42's command to give.
'The righteous is generous and gives'; coheres with the giving/lending ethic of v.42.
'He is ever lending generously'; the open-handed righteous of v.42.
'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' — direct citation of the love command, the cited half of the antithesis.
Commands not to seek the welfare of Ammon/Moab; one strand behind the popularly inferred 'hate your enemy' (no OT verse commands hatred per se).
'Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? ... I hate them with perfect hatred' — the scriptural posture of hating enemies Jesus overturns.
'Love the sojourner as yourself' — the love command already stretched beyond kin in the Holiness Code, anticipating love of enemies.
Return your enemy's stray ox; help the donkey of one who hates you — Torah's seed of active goodwill toward enemies.
'If your enemy is hungry, give him bread' — direct wisdom command to do good to enemies, behind 'love your enemies, do good.'
'Do not rejoice when your enemy falls' — renunciation of enmity coherent with loving enemies.
Job claims he never rejoiced at his enemy's ruin nor cursed him — pious refusal of vengeance behind the enemy-love ethic.
'Be holy, for I am holy' — the imitatio Dei formula directly behind 'be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect.'
'You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy' — the Holiness Code's call to imitate God, reframed as perfection in v.48.
'You shall be blameless/perfect (tamim) before the LORD your God' — the LXX 'teleios' here closely matches 'be perfect.'
'Walk before me and be blameless (tamim)' — the call to integrity before God behind 'be perfect.'
'The LORD is good to all, his mercy over all he has made' — God's indiscriminate goodness behind 'he makes his sun rise on evil and good.'
'Upon whom does his light not arise?' — God's light/sun given universally, paralleling v.45.
God waters the earth and provides rain abundantly; background to 'sends rain on the just and the unjust.'
God gives the rains in season for all; coheres with rain on just and unjust as common grace.
'You are children of the LORD your God' — divine-sonship language behind 'that you may be children of your Father.'
Be like a father to orphans and you will be like a son of the Most High — deuterocanonical sonship-through-mercy parallel to v.45.
